title: Vaccines and Your Rh Factor
learningGoals: Know how vaccines in pregnancy protect you and your newborn
Know when each recommended vaccine is given
Know your two options for protecting your baby from RSV
Understand what Rh-negative means for your pregnancy
Know when RhoGAM is given, and when to speak up

slides.heading: Vaccines and Your Rh Factor
onScreen: Prenatal Care
slides.narration: Welcome to the last lesson in Prenatal Care. We’ll cover two ways your care team helps protect your baby before birth: vaccines during pregnancy, and RhoGAM, a shot for people with Rh-negative blood. By the end, you’ll know what’s recommended, when, and what to ask.

visual.description: A pregnant person sitting in a bright clinic, smiling and chatting with a nurse after a vaccine, a small round bandage on her upper arm. Diverse people, soft teal and warm cream colors.

slides.heading: Two people protected by one shot
onScreen: Pregnancy makes some infections more serious for you
Your antibodies cross the placenta to your baby
Protection in the first months, before your baby can get these shots
slides.narration: Vaccines during pregnancy protect two people at once. Pregnancy changes your immune system, so illnesses like flu and COVID-19 can hit harder. When you get vaccinated, your body makes antibodies, and some of them cross the placenta to your baby. That gives your newborn protection in the first months of life, before they’re old enough to get these vaccines themselves.

slides.heading: Vaccines and when to get them
onScreen: Several can be given at the same visit
slides.narration: Here’s when each vaccine is usually given. Tdap, which protects against whooping cough, is given in every pregnancy, between twenty-seven and thirty-six weeks, ideally early in that window. The flu shot can be given in any trimester during flu season. The RSV vaccine is given between thirty-two and thirty-six weeks during RSV season. A COVID-19 vaccine can be given in any trimester. And if your first-visit blood work shows you're not immune to hepatitis B, you can start that vaccine series during pregnancy. Live vaccines, like MMR and chickenpox, aren’t given during pregnancy, so if you need them, you’ll get them after your baby is born. Several vaccines can be given at the same visit.
rows: Every pregnancy, 27 to 36 weeks, early in that window
If your first-visit blood test shows you’re not immune
Not during pregnancy; after birth if needed

slides.heading: Where recommendations stand
onScreen: Recommendations changed in 2025 and 2026
CDC: Tdap, flu, and RSV in pregnancy; COVID-19 for all adults
ACOG: all four, specifically during pregnancy
Ask your care team what’s right for you
slides.narration: You may have heard that vaccine recommendations have been changing, and that’s true. As of fall 2026, the CDC recommends Tdap, flu, and RSV vaccines during pregnancy, and a COVID-19 vaccine for all adults. The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists, the main group for pregnancy care doctors, recommends all four vaccines specifically during pregnancy. Guidance can change from season to season, so ask your care team which vaccines they recommend for you, and when.

slides.heading: RSV: two ways to protect your baby
onScreen: Option 1: RSV vaccine for you, 32 to 36 weeks
Option 2: an RSV antibody shot for your baby after birth
Most babies need only one
Had the RSV vaccine in a past pregnancy? Your baby gets the antibody shot
slides.narration: RSV is a common virus that can make young babies very sick. There are two ways to protect your newborn. You can get the RSV vaccine between thirty-two and thirty-six weeks during RSV season, which passes protection to your baby. Or your baby can get an RSV antibody shot after birth. Most babies need only one or the other. The RSV vaccine is given in only one pregnancy, so if you got it before, your baby will get the antibody shot instead. Talk with your care team about which option fits your due date.

question.prompt: You got a Tdap shot during your last pregnancy, two years ago. Do you need it again this pregnancy?
options: Yes, Tdap is recommended in every pregnancy
Only if your baby is born early
question.explanation: Tdap is recommended in every pregnancy, between 27 and 36 weeks, so each baby gets a fresh supply of antibodies against whooping cough.

slides.heading: What Rh-negative means
onScreen: Rh is a protein on red blood cells
Most people are Rh-positive
Checked with your first-visit blood work
Rh-negative parent + Rh-positive baby = a possible mismatch
Usually doesn’t harm this baby, but can affect future pregnancies
slides.narration: Now let’s talk about your Rh factor. Rh is a protein that can be on the surface of red blood cells. Most people have it, which makes them Rh-positive. People who don’t are Rh-negative. Your Rh factor is checked with your first-visit blood work. If you’re Rh-negative and your baby is Rh-positive, some of your baby’s blood can mix with yours, especially at birth. Your body may then make antibodies against Rh-positive blood. That usually doesn’t harm this baby, but in a future pregnancy, those antibodies can attack an Rh-positive baby’s red blood cells and cause serious anemia.

slides.heading: How RhoGAM protects future pregnancies
onScreen: A shot that keeps your body from making Rh antibodies
Around 28 weeks
Within 72 hours after birth, if your baby is Rh-positive
After bleeding, pregnancy loss, amniocentesis or CVS, or a hit to the belly
Some teams test your blood for the baby’s Rh type first
slides.narration: RhoGAM, also called Rh immune globulin, is a shot that keeps your body from making those antibodies. If you’re Rh-negative, you’ll usually get it around twenty-eight weeks. After birth, your baby’s blood type is checked, and if your baby is Rh-positive, you’ll get another dose within seventy-two hours. You may also need it any time your baby’s blood could mix with yours: after vaginal bleeding, a miscarriage or other pregnancy loss, an amniocentesis or CVS, or a fall or hit to your belly. Some care teams use a blood test to check your baby’s Rh type first, so you only get RhoGAM if your baby is Rh-positive.

visual.description: When RhoGAM is given: around 28 weeks, within 72 hours after birth if the baby is Rh-positive, after bleeding, pregnancy loss, or a procedure like amniocentesis, and after a fall or hit to the belly.

slides.heading: If you’re Rh-negative, speak up
onScreen: Know your blood type, and keep it with you
Call your care team for any bleeding
Call after a fall, car accident, or hit to your belly
In the ER or a new clinic, say: ’I’m Rh-negative and pregnant’
slides.narration: If you’re Rh-negative, it helps to speak up. Know your blood type and keep it in your phone. Call your care team if you have any bleeding, or after a fall, a car accident, or any hit to your belly, even if you feel fine. Your baby may need to be checked, and you may need RhoGAM. And if you ever go to an emergency room or a new clinic, tell them right away that you’re Rh-negative and pregnant.

question.prompt: You’re Rh-negative and 22 weeks pregnant. You slip and land hard on your belly, but you feel okay. What should you do?
options: Only call if you start bleeding
question.explanation: Call now, even if you feel fine. A hit to the belly is a reason to check on your baby, and you may need RhoGAM before 28 weeks.

slides.heading: Your vaccine and Rh notes
onScreen: Your blood type and Rh factor
Vaccines you’ve had this pregnancy, and dates
Vaccines still to plan
Your RSV plan: vaccine for you, or antibody for baby
slides.narration: Let’s put this in your Birth Readiness Brief. Write down your blood type and Rh factor, the vaccines you’ve had this pregnancy and when, the ones still to plan, and your RSV plan. Bring it to your next visit and to the hospital.

slides.heading: What we covered
onScreen: Vaccines in pregnancy protect you and your newborn
Tdap every pregnancy, 27 to 36 weeks; flu and COVID-19 any trimester
RSV: vaccine at 32 to 36 weeks, or an antibody shot for baby
Rh-negative: RhoGAM around 28 weeks and after birth if needed
Call for bleeding or a hit to the belly
slides.narration: Let’s recap. Vaccines during pregnancy protect you and give your newborn early protection. Tdap is given every pregnancy between twenty-seven and thirty-six weeks, and flu and COVID-19 vaccines can be given in any trimester. For RSV, you can get the vaccine at thirty-two to thirty-six weeks, or your baby can get an antibody shot after birth. If you’re Rh-negative, you’ll usually get RhoGAM around twenty-eight weeks and again after birth if your baby is Rh-positive. And call your care team for any bleeding or a hit to your belly. Next, a few review questions. Congratulations on finishing Prenatal Care.

reviewQuiz.prompt: How does a vaccine during pregnancy help your newborn?
options: It doesn’t; only you are protected
Your antibodies cross the placenta and protect your baby early on
It replaces all of your baby’s vaccines
reviewQuiz.explanation: Antibodies you make pass to your baby, protecting them in the first months, before they can get these vaccines themselves.

reviewQuiz.prompt: Which vaccine is NOT given during pregnancy?
reviewQuiz.explanation: MMR is a live vaccine, so it isn’t given during pregnancy. If you need it, you’ll get it after your baby is born.

reviewQuiz.prompt: You’re Rh-negative and your baby is born Rh-positive. When should you get RhoGAM?
options: Only if your baby is sick
reviewQuiz.explanation: RhoGAM within 72 hours after birth keeps your body from making antibodies that could affect a future pregnancy.
